lesson_title: The Tent, the Crane and the Fence
hook_text: Every scary graph equation is just a work order: push, lift, tighten. Read it like a builder, not a mathematician.
clip_script: This equation scares half of grade eleven: y equals two, times x minus one, all squared, minus eight. But it's not an equation. It's a work order for a construction crew. The basic parabola is a tent pitched at the town square. Now read the orders. The bracket, x minus one — that's the push crew. Which way? Don't guess — ask the bracket when it equals zero. At x equals one. So the tent pole moves to one: one step right. The minus eight at the end — that's the crane. Drop the whole tent eight metres. And the two out front — that's fabric tension. Pull the walls twice as steep. Done: the lowest point of the tent now stands at one, minus eight. You just read a turning point without a single calculation. And here's the free gift every tent gives you: symmetry. The two places the walls hit the ground — minus one and three — must sit evenly around the pole. Average them: one. The pole. If your intercepts don't average to the pole, one of them is lying to you. Push. Lift. Tension. Check the symmetry. Four moves, and the parabola works for you.
visual_style: A canvas tent on a sketched field: arrows pushing it right, a crane lowering it, ropes tightening the walls steeper; the two ground-contact points flashing and averaging back to the centre pole.
pacing: Playful open on the scary equation, deliberate beats for each crew order, brisk symmetric finish.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and read every graph equation like a work order.
